cards.a: LISP (Locator ID Separation Protocol) separates identity (EID) from location (RLOC): hosts keep stable IDs while mapping to current network locations through a map server/control plane. It is the control plane of SD-Access, enabling host mobility and policy without changing IPs.

cards.q: What do the terms EID and RLOC mean in LISP?
cards.a: EID (Endpoint Identifier) is the endpoint identity, typically the host IP, while RLOC (Routing Locator) is the current location, typically the site IP. A map translates EID to RLOC, so EIDs travel while RLOCs are the current location.

cards.q: What are the main LISP roles and devices?
cards.a: ITR (ingress tunnel router), ETR (egress tunnel router), MR/MS (map resolver/map server, the control plane), and PxTR (proxy, for interop with non-LISP networks). ITR/ETR are the edges; MS/MR is the control plane; PxTR handles legacy interop.

cards.q: What is the LISP mapping flow step by step?
cards.a: 1) The ITR needs a destination, 2) it sends a map-request to the MR/MS, 3) the MS returns the EID to RLOC mapping, and 4) the ITR encapsulates traffic to the ETR.

cards.q: What is the difference between the LISP control plane and data plane?
cards.a: The control plane performs the map lookup against the map server, while the data plane encapsulates traffic toward the resolved RLOC. Control = map lookup; data = encapsulation.

cards.q: How does LISP support SD-Access host mobility?
cards.a: LISP maps EIDs so hosts roam while keeping the same IP: the SD-Access control plane is LISP, the data plane is VXLAN, and the EID persists across moves.

cards.q: What are the benefits of LISP?
cards.a: Mobility (host keeps the same IP), scaling (splits the routing table), policy (mapping control), and interoperability with legacy networks through PxTR. LISP decouples routing scale from endpoint movement.

cards.q: Which commands verify and debug LISP operation?
cards.a: show lisp session, show lisp map-cache, show lisp eid-table, show lisp ipv4 database, show lisp ipv4 map-cache, and debug lisp.

cards.q: How do you troubleshoot LISP mapping and mobility issues?
cards.a: No map means a problem with the MR/MS (check map-cache); broken mobility points to EID issues (check eid-table); legacy failures point to PxTR (check database); slow lookups to the cache (debug lisp); and a down session to the underlay.

cards.q: What is the LISP role misused as the control plane versus edges?
cards.a: A common trap: MS/MR (map server/map resolver) is the control plane, while ITR and ETR are the edge routers that encapsulate/decapsulate at ingress and egress. PxTR provides interoperability with non-LISP networks.

cards.q: Why can a LISP host roam without changing its IP?
cards.a: Because the EID (identity) stays constant and only the RLOC (location) changes; the map server keeps the EID-to-RLOC mapping updated, so the host keeps its IP while roaming.
